    Image|endswith:
      - '\winrar.exe'
      - '\rar.exe'
      - '\unrar.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'updater.rar'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\winrar.exe OR *\WinRAR.exe OR *\rar.exe OR *\unrar.exe) @CommandLine:(*updater.rar* OR *updater.RAR*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(winrar|rar|unrar)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/updater\.rar/i
| table([_time, aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe")) AND Processes.process="*updater.rar*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe")) AND Processes.process="*updater.rar*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Recurring scheduled task running RemoteLibUpdater.exe (BURNYBEAR persistence, 3-min cadence) AIInstallation High
Hunts the UAC-0099 persistence mechanism where LUNCHPOKE registers a scheduled task that launches RemoteLibUpdater.exe (BURNYBEAR) every three minutes. The binary name is campaign-unique and the high execution frequency (many launches/hour, typically via Task Scheduler/svchost) is the distinguishing signal. Rationale: RemoteLibUpdater.exe is a campaign-unique binary named in the article; the >=3 execution threshold captures the article's explicit 'every three minutes' scheduled-task cadence, which no legitimate updater mimics. Sigma omitted because this is a count/threshold aggregation. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fake-notepad-plugin-delivers.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-notepad-plus-plus-plugins-to-stealthily-install-malware/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1499
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-named internal updater utility coincidentally called RemoteLibUpdater.exe (unlikely)
  • Security tooling repeatedly relaunching a monitored process during testing
  • A crash-loop of a benign service producing many process starts
Suppression filter
| where not (SampleCmd has_any ("\\Program Files\\") and Parents has_any ("services.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate scheduled tasks on the host (schtasks /query or DeviceEvents) for a task pointing at RemoteLibUpdater.exe with a 3-minute trigger; note whether it launches with no arguments (BURNYBEAR resource-exhaustion path) versus loading InitTest.dll. 2) Contain: disable/delete the scheduled task, kill RemoteLibUpdater.exe, isolate the host, quarantine the binary. 3) Hunt: correlate to the NppExport.dll side-load and updater.rar extraction, and check for MATCHBOIL.V2 C2 egress from the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "RemoteLibUpdater.exe"
| summarize Executions=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Parents=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName), SampleCmd=any(ProcessCommandLine), FolderPath=any(FolderPath) by DeviceName, AccountName, SHA256
| where Executions >= 3  // task fires every 3 minutes -> many launches over the window
| order by Executions desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\RemoteLibUpdater.exe"
| summarize Executions=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Parents=make_set(ParentProcessName), SampleCmd=any(CommandLine) by Computer, Account, NewProcessName
| where Executions >= 3  // 3-minute recurrence produces many launches
| order by Executions desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\RemoteLibUpdater.exe OR *\remotelibupdater.exe OR *\REMOTELIBUPDATER.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\RemoteLibUpdater\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName], function=count(as=Executions))
| Executions>=3
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parents values(Processes.process) as cmds from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="RemoteLibUpdater.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count>=3
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parents values(Processes.process) as cmds from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="RemoteLibUpdater.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count>=3
BURNYBEAR (RemoteLibUpdater.exe) loading MATCHBOIL.V2 InitTest.dll AICommand & Control High
Hunts the final loader hand-off: RemoteLibUpdater.exe (BURNYBEAR) side-loading InitTest.dll, the modified C#-based MATCHBOIL.V2 loader that fetches secondary payloads. Both the loader binary and the DLL names are campaign-unique, making this a very high-fidelity terminal-stage detection. Rationale: Both RemoteLibUpdater.exe and InitTest.dll are unique names disclosed by CERT-UA/THN; their pairing in a single image-load event is essentially pathognomonic for MATCHBOIL.V2 execution. Falcon/Splunk fall back to the InitTest.dll file drop since image-load isn't in the provided FDR/CIM schema; Sentinel uses the RemoteLibUpdater.exe process-create proxy. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-notepad-plus-plus-plugins-to-stealthily-install-malware/ • https://cyberpress.org/hackers-weaponize-notepad-8-8-3/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated legitimate InitTest.dll used by a test harness in a dev environment
  • A security-product module coincidentally sharing the RemoteLibUpdater.exe name
  • EDR-replayed IOC test in a sandbox during purple-team exercises
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture InitTest.dll and RemoteLibUpdater.exe hashes and the loading directory; check DeviceNetworkEvents from RemoteLibUpdater.exe for MATCHBOIL.V2 C2 or Dropbox WinRAR retrieval. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, delete the 3-minute scheduled task, and quarantine both binaries. 3) Hunt: pivot org-wide on the InitTest.dll/RemoteLibUpdater.exe hashes and on NppExport.dll side-loads to find other compromised hosts.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "RemoteLibUpdater.exe"
| where FileName =~ "InitTest.dll"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\RemoteLibUpdater.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: BURNYBEAR Loading MATCHBOIL.V2 InitTest.dll (UAC-0099)

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

2026-07-23 5 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Dolphin X C2 beacon to thedolphinx.top / backend.thedolphinx.top build backend
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Single process mass-harvesting browser, wallet & password-manager credential stores (Dolphin X sweep) · [LLM] Single process harvesting developer & cloud secrets (.env, SSH keys, AWS/GCP/kube configs) · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Dolphin X C2 beacon to thedolphinx.top / backend.thedolphinx.top build backend AICommand & Control High
Hunts host connections and DNS resolutions to the Dolphin X operator infrastructure (thedolphinx.top, backend.thedolphinx.top — build/exfil backend on :8443) and connections originating from the known Dolphin X sample hash. High-fidelity because the domains and backend port are named and corroborated by multiple vendor write-ups. Rationale: Anchored on the named C2 domains thedolphinx.top / backend.thedolphinx.top and the build-backend port 8443 (per Varonis + The Register), plus the article's sample SHA256 as an initiating-process pivot. Corroborated by four independent second sources. Cross-checked against: • https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/07/22/sneaky-windows-stealer-targets-300-apps-gives-crims-an-ai-profiler-to-maximize-profits/ • https://www.technadu.com/dolphin-x-new-windows-stealer-uses-ai-to-rank-which-victims-are-worth-robbing/631754/ • https://gbhackers.com/windows-stealer-uses-ai-profiling/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / TI analyst intentionally sandboxing or resolving the IOC domain from a corporate host
  • Threat-intel feed connector or URL-scanning appliance proactively resolving newly-reported malicious domains
  • Web proxy or DNS sinkhole logging the domain as it blocks it (source is the security tool, not a victim)
  • Unrelated legitimate service coincidentally hosted on :8443 (filter requires the thedolphinx substring to avoid this)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and DeviceName !in~ ("soc-sandbox01","ti-scanner01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName/SHA256 making the connection; if it is not a browser/security tool and matches the sample hash, treat as confirmed. Pull the full DeviceNetworkEvents timeline for that host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block thedolphinx.top and backend.thedolphinx.top at DNS/proxy/firewall, and force-reset credentials for every account used on that machine (browsers, cloud CLIs, SSH). 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating process across all hosts, search DeviceFileEvents for the credential-store sweep (see companion UCs), and query for any other host resolving the domains in the last 30 days.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "thedolphinx.top"
    or InitiatingProcessSHA256 == "726e7fe23560fe03ea36163d5f510b494f41a78bf811c92ff219f64b4bfe2be0"
| extend BackendPort8443 = (RemotePort == 8443)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, BackendPort8443
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Name has "thedolphinx.top"
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIP=ClientIP, Indicator=Name, Detail=QueryTypeName),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationHostName has "thedolphinx.top" or RequestURL has "thedolphinx.top" or (DestinationPort == 8443 and DestinationHostName has "thedolphinx")
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=SourceHostName, SrcIP=SourceIP, Indicator=coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL), Detail=tostring(DestinationPort))
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Dolphin X C2 domain resolution (thedolphinx.top)
id: 6f3a9c1e-4d2b-4f7a-9c1e-2b7d5e8a3f10
description: DNS resolution of Dolphin X operator/build-backend infrastructure
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-dolphin-x-malware-uses-ai-to-rank-high-value-targets/
  - https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/07/22/sneaky-windows-stealer-targets-300-apps-gives-crims-an-ai-profiler-to-maximize-profits/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/23

  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    query|contains: 'thedolphinx.top'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon (@DestinationHostname:(*thedolphinx.top* OR *backend.thedolphinx.top*) OR (@EventID:3 AND @DestinationPort:8443 AND @DestinationHostname:*thedolphinx*))
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/thedolphinx\.top$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

Single process mass-harvesting browser, wallet & password-manager credential stores (Dolphin X sweep) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects one non-machine-account process reading four or more distinct credential stores (Chromium/Gecko Login Data, wallet extension settings, desktop wallet keystores, KeePass vaults) within a 5-minute window — the Dolphin X stealer sweep across 9 browsers, 100+ wallet extensions, 65 desktop wallets and 10 password managers. Includes the known sample SHA256 as a booster. Rationale: Built from the article's explicit collection scope (9 browsers, 100+ wallet extensions, 65 desktop wallets, 10 password managers) expressed as a same-process fan-out across distinct credential file types in a tight window — the behaviour that distinguishes a stealer sweep from normal browser use. Sample SHA256 added as a high-confidence override. Cross-checked against: • https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/07/22/sneaky-windows-stealer-targets-300-apps-gives-crims-an-ai-profiler-to-maximize-profits/ • https://gbhackers.com/windows-stealer-uses-ai-profiling/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1555.005 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint backup / migration agents (e.g. profile-sync, browser-import tools) reading multiple browser profile files at once
  • Enterprise password-manager clients or browser-sync services touching vaults and Login Data
  • Antivirus / EDR full-disk scans opening credential SQLite files during a scheduled scan
  • Browser itself updating multiple profile stores after an upgrade
  • Forensic / DLP agents inventorying credential files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msmpeng.exe","mbamservice.exe","backup.exe","veeam.agent.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect InitiatingProcessFileName, folder path and SHA256 — a signed browser/backup tool is likely benign; an unsigned binary in %TEMP%/%APPDATA% or one matching the sample hash is malicious. Confirm the process also beaconed to thedolphinx.top. 2) Contain: isolate the host and reset all browser-saved, wallet, and password-manager credentials plus any crypto seed phrases; assume full compromise of stored secrets. 3) Hunt: pivot on the process SHA256 org-wide, check the developer-secret harvest UC for .env/.ssh/.aws access by the same process, and review outbound uploads to backend.thedolphinx.top.
let window = 5m;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileAccessed","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileCreated")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| extend LowerPath = tolower(FolderPath), LowerName = tolower(FileName)
| where (FileName in~ ("Login Data","Login Data For Account","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Web Data"))
    or (LowerPath has @"\local extension settings\")
    or (LowerName endswith ".kdbx")
    or (LowerPath has @"\ethereum\keystore")
| summarize DistinctStores = dcount(FileName), Stores = make_set(FolderPath, 25), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA256, bin(Timestamp, window)
| where DistinctStores >= 4 or InitiatingProcessSHA256 == "726e7fe23560fe03ea36163d5f510b494f41a78bf811c92ff219f64b4bfe2be0"
| order by FirstSeen desc
let window = 5m;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(ActingProcessName)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| extend LowerPath = tolower(TargetFilePath), LowerName = tolower(TargetFileName)
| where (TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Web Data"))
    or (LowerPath has @"\local extension settings\")
    or (LowerName endswith ".kdbx")
    or (LowerPath has @"\ethereum\keystore")
| summarize DistinctStores = dcount(TargetFileName), Stores = make_set(TargetFilePath, 25), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, window)
| where DistinctStores >= 4
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\Login Data* OR *\\key4.db* OR *\\logins.json* OR *\\cookies.sqlite* OR *\\Web Data* OR *\\Local Extension Settings\\* OR *.kdbx OR *\\ethereum\\keystore*)
#event_simpleName=/^(FileOpenInfo|FileWritten)$/
| TargetFileName=/(\\Login Data|\\key4\.db|\\logins\.json|\\cookies\.sqlite|\\Web Data|\\Local Extension Settings\\|\.kdbx$|\\ethereum\\keystore)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextProcessId, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true, as=DistinctStores))
| DistinctStores >= 4
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path dc(Filesystem.file_name) as distinct_stores min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN ("Login Data","key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Web Data") OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Local Extension Settings\\*" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.kdbx" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\ethereum\\keystore*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process_id _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where distinct_stores>=4 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Single process harvesting developer & cloud secrets (.env, SSH keys, AWS/GCP/kube configs) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects one non-machine-account process reading three or more distinct developer/cloud secret types (.env files, ~/.ssh private keys, .aws/credentials, gcloud config, .kube/config) within a 10-minute window — the Dolphin X developer/DevOps credential-collection capability that sets it apart from a commodity browser stealer. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's stated developer-secret theft (.env files, SSH keys, cloud access tokens, cloud CLI configs across 30+ cloud CLI tools) as a same-process multi-secret-type access burst — the DevOps-targeting angle that multiple sources call out as Dolphin X's distinguishing collection behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/07/22/sneaky-windows-stealer-targets-300-apps-gives-crims-an-ai-profiler-to-maximize-profits/ • https://www.technadu.com/dolphin-x-new-windows-stealer-uses-ai-to-rank-which-victims-are-worth-robbing/631754/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1528 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running a legit build/deploy that reads .env, ~/.ssh and cloud CLI configs (CI runners, terraform, kubectl, aws-cli sessions)
  • IDE / editor (VS Code) indexing a workspace containing .env and config files
  • Backup or endpoint-DLP agent scanning home directories
  • Secret-scanning security tools (gitleaks, trufflehog) walking dev machines
  • Configuration-management agent (Ansible/Chef) reading credential files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","terraform.exe","aws.exe","kubectl.exe","gcloud.exe","git.exe","python.exe","node.exe","ssh.exe","gitleaks.exe","trufflehog.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the InitiatingProcess is a known dev tool (code.exe, terraform.exe, aws.exe, kubectl.exe, git.exe) — those are usually benign; an unsigned binary in %TEMP%/%APPDATA%, or one matching the sample hash / beaconing to thedolphinx.top, is malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host and immediately rotate every exposed secret — SSH keys, AWS/GCP access keys, kube tokens, and any credentials in the read .env files — then review cloud audit logs (CloudTrail/GCP audit) for use of those keys from unfamiliar IPs. 3) Hunt: pivot on the process SHA256 org-wide and correlate with the browser/wallet sweep UC and outbound uploads to backend.thedolphinx.top:8443.
let window = 10m;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileAccessed","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileCreated")

Russian Espionage Group Exploited Zimbra Zero-Day to Steal Mail and 2FA Codes

The Hacker News
2026-07-23 21 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A Russian state-supported espionage group spent months reading Western mailboxes through a then-unknown flaw in Zimbra's webmail client. The payload goes after the last 90 days of email, the organization's entire email directory, the password saved in the browser and the codes kept for two-factor recovery. Opening the message was enough to start it. The NSA, CISA and partner agencies published

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Zimbra app-specific password 'ZimbraWeb' minted via CreateAppSpecificPasswordRequest · [LLM] Zimbra IMAP silently enabled (zimbraPrefImapEnabled=TRUE) for MFA-less mailbox access · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Russian Espionage Group Exploited Zimbra Zero-Day to Steal Mail and 2FA Codes
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ZimReaper C2/DNS callout to TA488 Zimbra-themed infrastructure (CVE-2025-66376) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ZimReaper DNS-tunnel exfiltration via long random subdomains of actor domains · [LLM] Zimbra 2FA scratch-code theft via GetScratchCodesRequest SOAP call · [LLM] ZimReaper Global Address List brute-force enumeration (two-character SOAP sweep) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
ZimReaper C2/DNS callout to TA488 Zimbra-themed infrastructure (CVE-2025-66376) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint DNS resolution and network connections to the nine TA488/ZimReaper C2 domains and nine C2 IPs used to exfiltrate stolen Zimbra mail, passwords and 2FA scratch codes. Article-specific because it pins the exact adversary infrastructure that Unit 42 (CL-STA-1114) and Proofpoint (TA488) both attributed to the same servers. Rationale: Uses the nine domains and nine IPs that The Hacker News confirmed appear in BOTH Unit 42's and Proofpoint's indicator lists (same infrastructure ties CL-STA-1114 to TA488), so these are second-source-validated IOCs, not single-article claims. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-204a • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits • https://securityaffairs.com/189673/security/russian-apt-targets-ukraine-via-zimbra-xss-flaw-cve-2025-66376.html
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / IR analyst detonating a sample in a sandbox on a monitored host
  • Threat-intel enrichment platform actively resolving IOC domains for feeds
  • Typosquat-lookalike legitimate 'emailanalytics.com' marketing traffic vs the '.com.ua' actor domain — verify exact TLD
  • A defender's own C2 sinkhole or DNS-block-page infrastructure resolving these names
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") and RemoteUrl != "emailanalytics.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host + initiating process (a browser rendering Zimbra webmail is expected for ZimReaper) and the exact indicator hit; confirm the domain TLD/IP matches the IOC list exactly. 2) Contain: block the domain/IP at DNS and egress, isolate the host, and treat every Zimbra mailbox that host authenticated to as compromised — reset password, kill active sessions, regenerate 2FA scratch codes. 3) Hunt: pivot on the src IP across all DNS logs for the long-random-subdomain exfil pattern, and query /opt/zimbra/log/audit.log for CreateAppSpecificPassword('ZimbraWeb') and GetScratchCodesRequest tied to that user.

let C2IPs = dynamic(["37.120.247.228","64.226.124.190","104.248.134.194","185.86.79.95","193.238.152.66","194.156.103.193","216.252.238.18","216.252.238.64","216.252.238.104"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (C2IPs) or RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

description: Detects DNS resolution of TA488/ZimReaper C2 domains used to exfiltrate stolen Zimbra mail and 2FA codes (CVE-2025-66376).

ZimReaper DNS-tunnel exfiltration via long random subdomains of actor domains AIActions on Objectives Medium
Behavioral hunt for the ZimReaper exfiltration channel: the payload encodes stolen CSRF tokens, browser passwords, 2FA scratch codes and mailbox data into many long high-entropy subdomains under actor domains (e.g. js-l1wt597cimk.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua). Distinct from the IOC-match UC because it catches NEW subdomains/hosts by shape, not by a fixed list. Rationale: Anchors on the two observed staging/exfil hosts (js-l1wt597cimk / js-26tik3egye4 .i.zimbrasoft.com.ua) which share the pattern of a 12-char random label under the actor's registered domains — the article states exfil is 'over DNS queries' with 'long random subdomain lookups'. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits • https://www.seqrite.com/blog/operation-ghostmail-zimbra-xss-russian-apt-ukraine/
ATT&CKT1048.003 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately re-registered actor domain now serving benign parked/CDN content with random-looking hostnames
  • Internal DNS resolver/forwarder aggregating many clients' queries into one ClientIP inflating the distinct count
  • Security scanner probing the domains generating varied subdomain lookups
  • CDN or ESP using genuinely long hashed subdomains under a lookalike domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe") and DeviceName !contains "dns"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent domain is one of the actor domains and inspect the subdomain labels for base32/hex encoding rather than dictionary words; identify the initiating browser process and the Zimbra user session. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the parent domain at the resolver, isolate the host, and force credential + 2FA-scratch-code rotation for the affected mailbox. 3) Hunt: decode a sample of the subdomains if possible, and check /opt/zimbra/log/audit.log for the preceding GetScratchCodesRequest / CreateAppSpecificPassword calls from the same account to confirm the full ZimReaper chain.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl endswith "zimbrasoft.com.ua" or RemoteUrl endswith "zimbra-metadata.com" or RemoteUrl endswith "zmailanalytics.com" or RemoteUrl endswith "emailanalytics.com.ua"
| extend Leftmost = tostring(split(RemoteUrl, ".")[0])
| summarize DistinctSubdomains = dcount(RemoteUrl), MaxLabelLen = max(strlen(Leftmost)), SampleHost = any(RemoteUrl), First = min(Timestamp), Last = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where DistinctSubdomains > 20 or MaxLabelLen >= 12   // ZimReaper encodes stolen data into many long (>=12 char) random subdomains; benign autocomplete/telemetry to one host stays low
| order by DistinctSubdomains desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Name endswith "zimbrasoft.com.ua" or Name endswith "zimbra-metadata.com" or Name endswith "zmailanalytics.com" or Name endswith "emailanalytics.com.ua"
| extend Leftmost = tostring(split(Name, ".")[0])
| summarize DistinctSubdomains = dcount(Name), MaxLabelLen = max(strlen(Leftmost)), SampleHost = any(Name), First = min(TimeGenerated), Last = max(TimeGenerated) by ClientIP, Computer
| where DistinctSubdomains > 20 or MaxLabelLen >= 12   // high-entropy long-label subdomains = DNS-tunnel exfil
| order by DistinctSubdomains desc
source:windows.sysmon @DestinationHostname:(*.zimbrasoft.com.ua OR *.zimbra-metadata.com OR *.zmailanalytics.com OR *.emailanalytics.com.ua)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| DomainName=/\.(zimbrasoft\.com\.ua|zimbra-metadata\.com|zmailanalytics\.com|emailanalytics\.com\.ua)$/i
| leftmost := splitString(DomainName, by=".", index=0)
| label_len := length(leftmost)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=[count(field=DomainName, distinct=true, as=distinct_subdomains), max(label_len, as=max_label_len)])
| distinct_subdomains > 20 OR max_label_len >= 12
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count dc(DNS.query) as distinct_subdomains from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="*.zimbrasoft.com.ua" OR DNS.query="*.zimbra-metadata.com" OR DNS.query="*.zmailanalytics.com" OR DNS.query="*.emailanalytics.com.ua") by DNS.src DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | eval leftmost=mvindex(split(query,"."),0) | eval label_len=len(leftmost) | stats sum(count) as queries dc(query) as distinct_subdomains max(label_len) as max_label_len values(query) as sample by src | where distinct_subdomains > 20 OR max_label_len >= 12
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(DNS.query) as distinct_subdomains from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="*.zimbrasoft.com.ua" OR DNS.query="*.zimbra-metadata.com" OR DNS.query="*.zmailanalytics.com" OR DNS.query="*.emailanalytics.com.ua") by DNS.src DNS.query | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | eval leftmost=mvindex(split(query,"."),0) | eval label_len=len(leftmost) | stats sum(count) as queries dc(query) as distinct_subdomains max(label_len) as max_label_len values(query) as sample by src | where distinct_subdomains > 20 OR max_label_len >= 12
Zimbra app-specific password 'ZimbraWeb' minted via CreateAppSpecificPasswordRequest AIInstallation High
Alerts on ZimReaper's persistence primitive: a SOAP CreateAppSpecificPasswordRequest that mints an app-specific password named ZimbraWeb, which grants IMAP/POP3/SMTP access without 2FA and survives password resets. This is the single highest-fidelity host-side IOC from Proofpoint's and Seqrite's guidance. Rationale: The credential name 'ZimbraWeb' is an exact, attacker-chosen string that Proofpoint says to grep /opt/zimbra/log/audit.log for and remove — it is near-zero in normal use, making CreateAppSpecificPassword+ZimbraWeb a very high-fidelity, low-FP alert. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-204a
ATT&CKT1098 T1556.006
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately naming their own app password 'ZimbraWeb' (rare but possible — verify the source session/IP)
  • Admin bulk-provisioning app passwords during an IMAP client rollout
  • A migration/backup tool that creates app-specific passwords programmatically
  • Penetration-test or purple-team activity replaying the TTP
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full audit.log line — capture the target account, source IP and the session that issued the SOAP call; confirm the app password name is 'ZimbraWeb' (or a close variant). 2) Contain: delete the ZimbraWeb app-specific password immediately, disable IMAP/POP if not needed, reset the account password AND invalidate sessions (note: app passwords survive resets, so deletion is mandatory). 3) Hunt: search audit.log for the same account's GetScratchCodesRequest and zimbraPrefImapEnabled=TRUE changes, and check whether the mailserver later sent further exploit emails (compromised-relay reuse).
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "CreateAppSpecificPassword" and SyslogMessage has "ZimbraWeb"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog CreateAppSpecificPassword ZimbraWeb
APPLICATION
index=* sourcetype=zimbra:audit source="/opt/zimbra/log/audit.log" "CreateAppSpecificPassword" "ZimbraWeb" | rex field=_raw "account=(?<account>[^;\s]+)" | stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(_raw) as sample by host account | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Zimbra 2FA scratch-code theft via GetScratchCodesRequest SOAP call AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts on ZimReaper pulling the account's two-factor recovery (scratch) codes through Zimbra's own GetScratchCodesRequest SOAP API — a call that should be close to absent in normal operation. Stolen scratch codes let the actor re-authenticate even after a password reset and session revocation. Rationale: Proofpoint explicitly recommends alerting on GetScratchCodesRequest because it 'should be close to absent in normal use'; ZimReaper calls it through the platform's own APIs, so any occurrence is a strong credential-access signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-204a
ATT&CKT1111 T1539
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately viewing/regenerating their own 2FA backup codes in account settings
  • Helpdesk-assisted 2FA recovery for a locked-out user
  • Zimbra admin auditing or migrating TOTP settings
  • Security-assessment tooling exercising the SOAP endpoint
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the target account and source IP from the audit.log entry; determine whether the request came from the user's normal browser/IP or from a webmail session correlated with an inbound HTML email view. 2) Contain: regenerate (invalidate) the account's 2FA scratch codes, reset the password, and revoke active sessions; check for any co-occurring ZimbraWeb app password and delete it. 3) Hunt: correlate the same account/session against DNS logs for the ZimReaper exfil domains and audit.log for zimbraPrefImapEnabled flips within the same time window.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "GetScratchCodesRequest"
| summarize Count = count(), Sample = any(SyslogMessage), First = min(TimeGenerated), Last = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, ProcessName
| order by Last desc
source:linux.syslog GetScratchCodesRequest
APPLICATION
index=* sourcetype=zimbra:audit source="/opt/zimbra/log/audit.log" "GetScratchCodesRequest" | rex field=_raw "account=(?<account>[^;\s]+)" | rex field=_raw "oip=(?<src_ip>[0-9a-fA-F\.:]+)" | stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(src_ip) as src_ip by host account | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Zimbra IMAP silently enabled (zimbraPrefImapEnabled=TRUE) for MFA-less mailbox access AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Seqrite-observed persistence step where ZimReaper flips zimbraPrefImapEnabled to TRUE so the minted app-specific password can reach the mailbox over IMAP without 2FA. Article-specific because it pairs the exact attribute name with the ZimbraWeb app-password TTP. Rationale: Seqrite's January case documented the payload flipping zimbraPrefImapEnabled to TRUE; combined with the ZimbraWeb app password this is the mechanism for durable MFA-less IMAP access, so the literal attribute string is a high-value hunt anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.seqrite.com/blog/operation-ghostmail-zimbra-xss-russian-apt-ukraine/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-204a
ATT&CKT1098 T1556
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User enabling IMAP themselves to add a desktop/mobile mail client
  • Admin bulk-enabling IMAP via a COS (class of service) policy change
  • Mail-migration project turning IMAP on across many accounts
  • Provisioning automation setting mailbox prefs at account creation
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the account and whether the change came from an admin console session or a user webmail session; check the timestamp against any inbound HTML email view for that user. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, set zimbraPrefImapEnabled back to FALSE, delete any ZimbraWeb app password, reset credentials and regenerate 2FA scratch codes. 3) Hunt: enumerate all accounts with zimbraPrefImapEnabled=TRUE that have no business need for IMAP (per Proofpoint guidance) and cross-check them against the GetScratchCodesRequest and app-password alerts.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "zimbraPrefImapEnabled" and SyslogMessage has "TRUE"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog zimbraPrefImapEnabled TRUE
APPLICATION
index=* sourcetype=zimbra:audit source="/opt/zimbra/log/audit.log" "zimbraPrefImapEnabled" "TRUE" | rex field=_raw "account=(?<account>[^;\s]+)" | stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(_raw) as sample by host account | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
ZimReaper Global Address List brute-force enumeration (two-character SOAP sweep) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects ZimReaper's directory-harvest step: it brute-forces the Global Address List by querying every two-character combination until the entire directory is returned, producing a burst of GAL search SOAP requests from a single Zimbra session far above normal autocomplete usage. Rationale: The article states the payload 'brute-forces the Global Address List, querying every two-character combination until the whole list comes back' — a volumetric GAL-search pattern that a per-session count threshold on the SearchGalRequest SOAP op surfaces cleanly. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/russian-espionage-group-exploited.html • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/ta488-targets-zimbra-mailservers-half-click-exploits
ATT&CKT1087.003 T1087
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Large mail-merge or CRM sync tool enumerating the GAL for contact caching
  • A newly onboarded user's client aggressively pre-caching the directory
  • Admin address-book export or bulk-provisioning script
  • A shared-account/kiosk session generating many autocomplete lookups
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the query source is a single user session and inspect whether the search terms iterate systematically through two-character strings (a→az, etc.) rather than real name fragments. 2) Contain: terminate the session, reset the account and rotate 2FA scratch codes; if the account is confirmed compromised, treat the whole GAL as harvested. 3) Hunt: correlate the session with GetScratchCodesRequest / CreateAppSpecificPassword(ZimbraWeb) calls and with outbound DNS to the actor domains within the same window to confirm ZimReaper rather than a benign bulk tool.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "SearchGalRequest"
| summarize GalQueries = count(), Sample = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where GalQueries > 100   // two-char enumeration ~ 36^2 (>1200) requests; normal autocomplete rarely exceeds a handful per 10m
| order by GalQueries desc
source:linux.syslog SearchGalRequest
APPLICATION
index=* sourcetype=zimbra:audit source="/opt/zimbra/log/audit.log" "SearchGalRequest" | rex field=_raw "account=(?<account>[^;\s]+)" | bin _time span=10m | stats count as gal_queries by _time host account | where gal_queries > 100 | sort - gal_queries
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("37.120.247.228", "64.226.124.190", "104.248.134.194", "185.86.79.95", "193.238.152.66", "194.156.103.193", "216.252.238.18", "216.252.238.64", "216.252.238.104") or RemoteUrl has_any ("analyticemailmeter.com", "emailanalytics.com.ua", "istc-cloud.com", "mailnalysis.com", "synacorzimbra.nl", "zimbra-metadata.com", "zimbrastat.com", "zimbrasoft.com.ua", "zmailanalytics.com", "js-l1wt597cimk.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,

let BadIPs     = dynamic(["37.120.247.228", "64.226.124.190", "104.248.134.194", "185.86.79.95", "193.238.152.66", "194.156.103.193", "216.252.238.18", "216.252.238.64", "216.252.238.104"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["analyticemailmeter.com", "emailanalytics.com.ua", "istc-cloud.com", "mailnalysis.com", "synacorzimbra.nl", "zimbra-metadata.com", "zimbrastat.com", "zimbrasoft.com.ua", "zmailanalytics.com", "js-l1wt597cimk.i.zimbrasoft.com.ua"]);

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1176
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: registry_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetObject|contains:
            - '\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Group-policy-managed extension whitelists
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")
    by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-66376")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-66376")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-66376")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-66376")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

SecurityEvent
