DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries Command & Control Medium
Long subdomain labels + frequent queries to a single 2LD = DNS C2/exfil.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 53 and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend qlen = strlen(RemoteUrl)
| where qlen > 50
| extend SecondLevelDomain = extract(@"([\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,})$", 1, RemoteUrl)
| summarize qcount = count(), uniqueSubs = dcount(RemoteUrl), maxLabel = max(qlen)
    by DeviceName, SecondLevelDomain
| where qcount > 100 and uniqueSubs > 20
| order by qcount desc
// ASIM ImDnsActivity normalises Windows DNS, Sysmon EID 22, Linux dnsmasq, etc.
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DnsQueryTypeName == "TXT"
| summarize Queries = count(), DistinctNames = dcount(DnsQuery)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Queries > 200    // tune to TXT-query baseline for environment
| order by Queries desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT

    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-23 14 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

In the second quarter of 2026, the continuing effects of Microsoft’s disruption of the Tycoon2FA phishing platform contributed to sustained declines in several major phishing techniques, while threat actors expanded into Teams-based social engineering and employed increasingly automated and multi-stage attack chains. The post Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

ATT&CKT1059.001 T1190 T1204.004 T1528 T1566 T1566.001
Domains9i6pokerdepot.com t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound malware campaign email from DKIM-signed sender 9i6pokerdepot.com · [LLM] Second-stage BAT dropper retrieval from ClickUp attachment subdomain t90141296286 · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] BAT-spawned hidden PowerShell pulling installer from pixeldrain.com · [LLM] LOLBin download of installer.exe from pixeldrain.com API to user Temp · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Inbound malware campaign email from DKIM-signed sender 9i6pokerdepot.com AIDelivery High
Hunts the specific Q2 2026 automated malware-delivery campaign that abused a DKIM-signing sending domain (9i6pokerdepot.com / Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com) and addressed generic role-based mailboxes to deliver a nested-EML + calendar-invite lure. Anchors on the exact operator sender identity rather than generic phishing heuristics. Rationale: Sender domain/address 9i6pokerdepot.com and Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com are from the article IOC table (first/last seen 2026-06-15). External write-up confirmed the campaign targeted role-based mailboxes (ar, accountsreceivable, hr, payroll) and used a login.microsoftonline.com auth-redirect lure, making the sender identity a high-fidelity anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate business partner legitimately registers a lookalike gambling/finance domain (extremely unlikely for this exact string)
  • Security team replaying the phishing sample into a test tenant
  • Threat-intel/phish-simulation vendor sending a controlled test from a spoofed address
  • Internal forwarding of the original malicious mail as an attachment for reporting
Suppression filter
| where DeliveryLocation !in ("Quarantine","Blocked")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all EmailEvents for SenderFromDomain 9i6pokerdepot.com, note DeliveryAction/DeliveryLocation and whether any landed in Inbox vs quarantined; expand EmailAttachmentInfo for nested .eml/.ics. 2) Contain: soft-delete/purge delivered copies via Explorer, block the sender domain and Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com at the mail gateway, and check UrlClickEvents for any recipient clicks. 3) Hunt: for any clicker, pivot to the ClickUp/pixeldrain UCs below to confirm second-stage retrieval on their device.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderMailFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderFromAddress =~ "customer.service@9i6pokerdepot.com"
| join kind=leftouter (EmailAttachmentInfo | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | project NetworkMessageId, FileName, FileType) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails, AttachmentFile = FileName, AttachmentType = FileType, UrlCount
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderMailFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderFromAddress =~ "customer.service@9i6pokerdepot.com"
| join kind=leftouter (EmailAttachmentInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | project NetworkMessageId, FileName, FileType) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails, AttachmentFile = FileName, AttachmentType = FileType, UrlCount
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Email.All_Email where (All_Email.src_user="customer.service@9i6pokerdepot.com" OR All_Email.src_user="*@9i6pokerdepot.com") by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.subject, All_Email.action, _time | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | sort - _time
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email.All_Email where (All_Email.src_user="customer.service@9i6pokerdepot.com" OR All_Email.src_user="*@9i6pokerdepot.com") by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.subject, All_Email.action, _time | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)` | sort - _time
Second-stage BAT dropper retrieval from ClickUp attachment subdomain t90141296286 AIDelivery High
Detects a host resolving/connecting to the campaign-specific ClickUp attachment subdomain t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com that hosted the Financial_report.bat dropper. Anchors on the unique campaign subdomain (not generic ClickUp SaaS traffic) so it does not fire on legitimate ClickUp usage. Rationale: t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com and the URL path fragment fb39c3a9-3161-40ad are the exact stage-2 BAT dropper indicators from the article IOC table; the campaign-unique subdomain avoids FPs from normal ClickUp use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/
ATT&CKT1105 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.All_Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user who legitimately owns ClickUp workspace t90141296286 downloads their own attachment (implausible given campaign attribution)
  • Security analyst detonating the sample in an internet-connected sandbox on a monitored host
  • Web proxy or SWG pre-fetching/scanning the URL from an appliance IP
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling automatically resolving the IOC
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host+user and the initiating process for the connection; confirm whether a .bat/.exe file was written (DeviceFileEvents FileOriginUrl containing clickup-attachments.com). 2) Contain: isolate the device, block *.clickup-attachments.com/t90141296286 at the proxy, and revoke the user's active sessions. 3) Hunt: chase the process-tree UC (BAT -> hidden PowerShell -> pixeldrain) and the pixeldrain installer UC on the same host and across the org.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com" or (RemoteUrl has "clickup-attachments.com" and RemoteUrl has "fb39c3a9-3161-40ad")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BAT-spawned hidden PowerShell pulling installer from pixeldrain.com AIInstallation High
Detects the campaign's stage-2 to stage-3 execution chain: a .bat (Financial_report.bat) launched via cmd.exe spawning a hidden-window PowerShell that downloads installer.exe from pixeldrain.com into the user Temp directory. Anchors on the pixeldrain.com string inside a PowerShell command line spawned from a batch file. Rationale: pixeldrain.com/api/file/3v92oJiL is the article's stage-3 installer URL; a corroborating write-up and ANY.RUN reports confirm the chain is a .bat launching hidden PowerShell that fetches installer.exe from pixeldrain into Temp. The pixeldrain.com + hidden-window + .bat-parent combination is very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://any.run/report/84f73741867e012140103aa9eb59bfaef6bf8c02aa7b9579be7aad2143418c03/18abf34d-1f07-4902-8343-13b9f8358605

  • Malware analyst reproducing the chain on an instrumented host
  • Red-team operation emulating this exact campaign
  • A power user pasting a pixeldrain link into a PowerShell one-liner to grab a shared file
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ".bat" or HiddenWindow == true
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full PowerShell command line and parent chain; confirm the download target (installer.exe) and whether it wrote to %TEMP%. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the PowerShell/installer processes, and quarantine any dropped installer.exe/.bat; reset the user's credentials/sessions. 3) Hunt: pivot on the dropped installer's SHA256 across the fleet, check DeviceNetworkEvents to pixeldrain.com, and correlate back to the 9i6pokerdepot.com email and ClickUp download.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "pixeldrain.com" or ProcessCommandLine has "3v92oJiL"
| extend HiddenWindow = ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-w(in(dowstyle)?)?\s+h(idden)?"
| extend BatParent = InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ".bat" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "financial_report"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, HiddenWindow, BatParent, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has "pixeldrain.com" or CommandLine has "3v92oJiL"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LOLBin download of installer.exe from pixeldrain.com API to user Temp AIInstallation Medium
Network/file pivot for the stage-3 payload: a LOLBin (PowerShell/curl/bitsadmin/certutil) connecting to pixeldrain.com/api/file and dropping installer.exe into the user Temp directory, with the dropper self-deleting on exit. Catches the download even when the PowerShell command line does not capture the URL string. Rationale: pixeldrain.com/api/file/3v92oJiL is the article's final-installer IOC; corroboration shows the dropper fetched installer.exe into %TEMP%, ran it silently, then self-deleted. Scoping pixeldrain contact to LOLBins + Temp .exe drop keeps this high-signal despite pixeldrain being a public file host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://any.run/report/e0b7a89ed43ccab4251a859ace10db649fe23d864f0129599b7cd4994d44cc3f/d90e56a9-0adf-452f-a2a9-912430d09f50
ATT&CKT1105 T1102
Data sourcesWeb.All_Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user genuinely downloading a shared file from pixeldrain via browser (excluded here by requiring a LOLBin initiator)
  • Developer using curl/bitsadmin to fetch a legitimate pixeldrain-hosted artifact
  • Automated build/test agent pulling a dependency mirror from pixeldrain
  • Security tooling detonating/scanning the pixeldrain URL from a monitored host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the LOLBin initiator and whether an .exe landed in %TEMP% (DroppedFile/SHA256 from the join); check if the file was subsequently deleted (self-delete artifact). 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine/collect the installer.exe (before self-delete if possible), block pixeldrain.com/api/file at proxy, and reset user sessions. 3) Hunt: sweep the installer SHA256 org-wide, review persistence (Run keys/scheduled tasks) created after execution, and correlate to the 9i6pokerdepot.com sender and ClickUp subdomain UCs.
let DownloadHosts = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where RemoteUrl has "pixeldrain.com" and (RemoteUrl has "/api/file" or RemoteUrl has "3v92oJiL")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","mshta.exe")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP;
DownloadHosts
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName endswith ".exe" and FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp")
    | project FileTimestamp = Timestamp, DeviceId, DroppedFile = FileName, DroppedPath = FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, SHA256
  ) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, DroppedFile, DroppedPath, FileOriginUrl, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "pixeldrain.com" and (Url has "/api/file" or Url has "3v92oJiL")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, DstHostname, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

references:

detection:

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\curl.exe OR *\bitsadmin.exe OR *\certutil.exe OR *\mshta.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\CertUtil.exe) @DestinationHostname:pixeldrain.com

| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web.All_Web where (All_Web.url="*pixeldrain.com/api/file*" OR All_Web.url="*3v92oJiL*") by All_Web.src, All_Web.user, All_Web.dest, All_Web.url, All_Web.http_user_agent, _time | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Web)` | sort - _time
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web.All_Web where (All_Web.url="*pixeldrain.com/api/file*" OR All_Web.url="*3v92oJiL*") by All_Web.src, All_Web.user, All_Web.dest, All_Web.url, All_Web.http_user_agent, _time | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Web)` | sort - _time
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Auth.js v5 fail-open trigger: server-configuration error emitted in app logs AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact Auth.js/next-auth v5 configuration-error log lines (InvalidEndpoints, MissingSecret/AUTH_SECRET, or the generic 'problem with the server configuration' message) that flip the auth() wrapper into returning a truthy error object instead of null. Once this appears, any middleware using existence-only checks (!!auth / if(req.auth)) fails open and treats every request as authenticated. Rationale: Uses the advisory's verbatim strings: the '[auth][error]' prefix, the named error classes 'InvalidEndpoints' and 'MissingSecret'/'AUTH_SECRET', and the surfaced message 'problem with the server configuration'. These are high-fidelity because they are Auth.js internal error identifiers that appear only when the configuration breaks — the precise precondition for the fail-open state. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3 • https://authjs.dev/reference/core/errors • https://authjs.dev/getting-started/session-management/protecting
ATT&CKT1556
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Transient config error during a rolling deploy that is corrected within seconds (env var briefly unset)
  • Non-production/staging hosts intentionally running with an incomplete provider config
  • A monitoring or documentation tool echoing the error text back into logs
  • Local developer environment logs shipped to the same index
  • Deliberate chaos/DR testing of the auth layer
Suppression filter
| where Computer !has "staging" and Computer !has "dev" and HostName !has "preview"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the app is on a vulnerable next-auth build (>=5.0.0-beta.0, <=5.0.0-beta.31) and that middleware uses existence-only checks (!!auth / if(req.auth)) rather than !!req.auth?.user; identify the affected host/environment and whether it is internet-facing. 2) CONTAIN: Restore the missing env var (AUTH_SECRET / provider issuer|authorization) or roll back the deploy; if it is production and internet-facing, gate traffic at the LB until fixed and apply the documented workaround (check req.auth?.user). 3) HUNT: Pull access logs for the error window and look for successful (200/302) requests to protected routes from sessions with no auth cookie — pivot to UC 'Auth.js fail-open: protected-route access during a config-error window'.
// Auth.js config-error state that causes existence-based auth checks to fail open
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SyslogMessage has "[auth][error]"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("InvalidEndpoints", "MissingSecret", "AUTH_SECRET", "problem with the server configuration")
| summarize ErrorCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleLog = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, HostName, ProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Auth.js v5 Fail-Open Configuration Error (InvalidEndpoints / MissingSecret)
id: a4dbb25b-f4c7-5bdd-af42-49468d365b01
description: Detects Auth.js (next-auth v5) server-configuration errors that cause the auth() wrapper to return a truthy error object, making existence-based auth checks fail open (GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3
  - https://authjs.dev/reference/core/errors
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/24
tags:
  - attack.t1556
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  product: nodejs
  service: application
detection:
  selection_prefix:
    keywords:
      - '[auth][error]'
  selection_error:
    keywords:
      - 'InvalidEndpoints'
      - 'MissingSecret'
      - 'AUTH_SECRET'
      - 'problem with the server configuration'
  condition: selection_prefix and selection_error
level: high
"[auth][error]" AND ("InvalidEndpoints" OR "MissingSecret" OR "AUTH_SECRET" OR "problem with the server configuration")
# log group: /aws/lambda/<your-nextjs-app>  (or the ECS/app-runner app log group hosting Auth.js)
fields @timestamp, @logStream, @message
| filter @message like /\[auth\]\[error\]/ and @message like /(InvalidEndpoints|MissingSecret|AUTH_SECRET|problem with the server configuration)/
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 200
APPLICATION
index=* ("[auth][error]") ("InvalidEndpoints" OR "MissingSecret" OR "AUTH_SECRET" OR "problem with the server configuration")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(_raw) as sampleLog by host, source, sourcetype
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
Auth.js fail-open: protected-route access succeeds during a config-error window AIExploitation Medium
Correlates Auth.js '[auth][error]' log lines with successful (200/302) HTTP responses to protected application routes in the same short time window. During the config-error state the auth object is truthy for everyone, so unauthenticated requests to gated routes start returning success instead of redirect/401 — this catches the bypass being exercised, not just the enabling condition. Rationale: Ties the advisory's cause ('[auth][error]' -> truthy auth object) to its observable effect (protected routes returning 200/302 to requests that should have been denied). Scoping to /api/ excluding /api/auth targets application-protected routes without a customer-specific placeholder; the AnonReqs/empty-username count highlights sessions that succeeded without an authenticated user. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3 • https://authjs.dev/getting-started/session-management/protecting
ATT&CKT1556 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuinely public /api routes that are intentionally unauthenticated (health, webhooks, public content)
  • Config error and legitimate authenticated traffic simply coinciding in the same 5-minute bin
  • API routes that perform their own token/role check downstream and are not gated by the vulnerable middleware
  • Load-balancer or uptime-probe hitting API endpoints during the error window
  • Static/cached responses served without hitting the auth middleware
Suppression filter
| where not(CsUriStem in ("/api/health", "/api/healthz", "/api/ping", "/api/webhooks"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each flagged bin, pull the individual AppServiceHTTPLogs rows and check whether the succeeding requests carried a valid session cookie / CsUsername — no-cookie 200s to a gated route during an error window are true positives. 2) CONTAIN: Fix the underlying config (restore AUTH_SECRET / provider endpoints) or roll back; treat any data returned to unauthenticated callers as potentially exposed and revoke/rotate as needed. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every distinct source IP and path served during the window, and search for follow-on actions (data reads, privileged API calls) from those IPs after the fail-open period.
// Successful protected-route access occurring in the same 5-min bin as an Auth.js config error = fail-open exercised
let ErrBins = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where SyslogMessage has "[auth][error]"
    | extend Bin = bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
    | distinct Bin;
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ScStatus in (200, 302)
| where CsUriStem startswith "/api/" and not(CsUriStem startswith "/api/auth")
| extend Bin = bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| join kind=inner (ErrBins) on Bin
| summarize Requests = count(), Paths = make_set(CsUriStem, 20), SourceIPs = make_set(CIp, 50), AnonReqs = countif(isempty(CsUsername)) by Bin, CsHost
| order by Bin desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where Web.status IN ("200","302") Web.url="/api/*" NOT Web.url="/api/auth*" by _time span=5m, Web.site, Web.src, Web.url, Web.status
| rename Web.* as *
| join type=inner _time [
    search index=* "[auth][error]"
    | bin _time span=5m
    | stats count as authErrors by _time ]
| where authErrors > 0
| stats sum(count) as okProtectedReqs values(url) as urls values(src) as sourceIPs by _time, site
| sort - _time
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.status IN ("200","302") Web.url="/api/*" NOT Web.url="/api/auth*" by _time span=5m, Web.site, Web.src, Web.url, Web.status
| rename Web.* as *
| join type=inner _time [
    search index=* "[auth][error]"
    | bin _time span=5m
    | stats count as authErrors by _time ]
| where authErrors > 0
| stats sum(count) as okProtectedReqs values(url) as urls values(src) as sourceIPs by _time, site
| sort - _time
Auth.js: protected /api access returning success with no session cookie (fail-open evidence) AIExploitation Medium
Standalone hunt for the observable outcome of the bypass: successful (200/302) responses to protected application routes where the request carried NO Auth.js session cookie (authjs.session-token / __Secure-authjs.session-token). Under the vulnerable existence-only check, an unauthenticated request with no session cookie is granted access — this surfaces that outcome even without pairing to the error log. Rationale: Grounded in the advisory's core claim that access is granted to 'every request, including unauthenticated ones', combined with the known Auth.js v5 default session-cookie name 'authjs.session-token' (and its '__Secure-' HTTPS variant). A gated /api route returning 200/302 to a request with no session cookie and no authenticated user is the direct fingerprint of the fail-open. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3 • https://authjs.dev/getting-started/session-management/protecting
ATT&CKT1078 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately public /api endpoints that never require a session (health, public config, webhooks)
  • First request of a login flow before any session cookie is set
  • API keys / bearer-token auth used instead of session cookies (auth carried in Authorization header, not the cookie)
  • Access logs that do not capture the Cookie header, causing every row to look cookie-less
  • CDN/edge-cached API responses served without the origin auth middleware
Suppression filter
| where not(CsUriStem in ("/api/health", "/api/healthz", "/api/ping", "/api/webhooks", "/api/public"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the flagged /api paths are actually meant to be authenticated (not public); check whether auth is expected via Authorization header rather than cookie before calling it a bypass. 2) CONTAIN: If confirmed, apply the Auth.js fix/workaround (check req.auth?.user, restore config) and revoke exposure; block the offending source IPs if abuse is evident. 3) HUNT: Cross-reference these no-cookie successes against '[auth][error]' log windows to confirm causation, and review what data/actions those requests obtained to scope the exposure.
// Protected /api routes returning success to a request that carried NO Auth.js session cookie
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ScStatus in (200, 302)
| where CsUriStem startswith "/api/" and not(CsUriStem startswith "/api/auth")
| where isempty(Cookie) or Cookie !contains "authjs.session-token"
| where isempty(CsUsername)
| summarize Requests = count(), Paths = make_set(CsUriStem, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by CsHost, CIp
| where Requests > 0
| order by LastSeen desc
CLOUD
index=* sourcetype=*:access* (status=200 OR status=302) uri_path="/api/*" NOT uri_path="/api/auth*" NOT cookie="*authjs.session-token*"
| stats count as reqs values(uri_path) as paths dc(src_ip) as srcIPs by host, src_ip
| where reqs > 0
| sort - reqs
